Abstract:
Ensuring the safety of physical human–robot interaction (pHRI) is of utmost importance for industries and organisations seeking to incorporate robots into their workspaces. To address this concern, the ISO/TS 15066:2016 outlines hazard analysis and preventive measures for ensuring safety in Human–Robot Collaboration (HRC). To analyse human–robot contact, it is common practice to separately evaluate the “transient” and “quasi-static” contact phases. Accurately measuring transient forces during close human–robot collaboration requires so-called “biofidelic” sensors that closely mimic human tissue properties, featuring adequate bandwidth and balanced damping. The dynamics of physical human–robot interactions using biofidelic measuring devices are being explored in this research. In this paper, one biofidelic sensor is tested to analyse its dynamic characteristics and identify the main factors influencing its performance and its practical applications for testing. To this aim, sensor parameters, such as natural frequency and damping coefficient, are estimated by utilising a custom physical pendulum setup to impact the sensor. Mathematical models developed to characterise the sensor system and pendulum dynamics are also disclosed.

Abstract:
Collaborative robots (cobots) can be employed in close proximity to human workers without safety fences. The operation mode Power and Force Limiting requires that cobots not exceed the biomechanical limits of ISO/TS 15066 to ensure protection against injuries caused by collisions with them. Collision tests must be performed to prove that cobots cannot exceed the biomechanical limits. Such tests are performed with a biofidelic measuring device that measures contact forces and replicates the biomechanics of the human body. Biomechanical response curves serve as a reference for the calibration of such devices. In order to be able to compare measurements and limits correctly and reliably, the limits and response curves for calibration must be obtained from the same data with the same methodology. In this article, we present a new technique for developing biomechanical response curves, which employs a statistical model we used to calculate biomechanical limits for cobots in a previous study. This technique's development process entails normalizing the data over force, resampling them and then fitting the newly obtained samples to a log-normal distribution. The statistical model makes it possible to produce response curves for the same quantile we used for the limits. Our technique adds a confidence region around each response curve to express the sufficiency of the available data. We have produced response curves for 24 different body locations for which we have calculated limits. These curves will enable manufacturers of cobot testing equipment to calibrate their measuring devices precisely.

The excerpt supports the conclusion that when a cable-driven robot loses motor power, its cables can backdrive the actuator unless a self-locking or braking mechanism is present. In the described tensegrity robot, merely holding a pose normally requires continued motor input specifically to prevent cable backdriving. The proposed mitigation is a multistage braking system: a passive Bi-Directional Self-Locking Clutch (BDSLC) handles routine pose holding and blocks output loads from driving the input, while a heavy-duty Retractable Jaw Clutch is intended for large impact events. Because the BDSLC requires no input power, motors can be shut down while the robot remains secured, reducing power consumption. The excerpt provides partial information relevant to what may happen to a robot arm when power is lost, primarily through its discussion of back-drivability, gearing, and compliance. A back-drivable actuator permits forces applied at the arm output to move the actuator input; actuators with high back-drivability require only a small output torque or force, while low-back-drivability systems—often caused by high gear ratios—require substantially more force. In contrast, non-back-drivable mechanisms such as motors with lead screws cannot rotate the output unless the input rotates first, so they may resist passive movement after de-energization. The excerpt also states that compliant actuators move under external force and are favored because they reduce impact forces, limit damage, and improve safety and comfort. However, it does not specify the arm’s drop distance or speed under gravity after power loss, nor does it discuss particular mitigations such as rest poses, UPS-backed controllers, mechanical brakes, controlled stopping before de-energizing, or supported park positions. Abstract:
<jats:p>The past decade has witnessed remarkable advancements in autonomous systems, such as automobiles that are evolving from traditional vehicles to ones capable of navigating complex environments without human intervention. Similarly, the rise of self-driving laboratories, which leverage robotics and artificial intelligence to accelerate discovery, is driving a paradigm shift in scientific research. As SDLs evolve to expand the scope of chemical processes that can be performed, it is essential to bring safety to the forefront of SDL research to ensure necessary safeguards against potential accidents that range from near-misses to catastrophic failures. This perspective examines the trajectory of self-driving laboratories, juxtaposing their development with those of other autonomous technologies, with a particular focus on safety. We explore current safety status and concerns, identify opportunities for innovation to shape this rapidly evolving landscape, and reflect on the actions the SDL community can take moving forward.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This article attempts to bridge the gap between widely discussed ethical principles of Human-centered AI (HCAI) and practical steps for effective governance. Since HCAI systems are developed and implemented in multiple organizational structures, I propose 15 recommendations at three levels of governance: team, organization, and industry. The recommendations are intended to increase the reliability, safety, and trustworthiness of HCAI systems: (1) reliable systems based on sound software engineering practices, (2) safety culture through business management strategies, and (3) trustworthy certification by independent oversight. Software engineering practices within teams include audit trails to enable analysis of failures, software engineering workflows, verification and validation testing, bias testing to enhance fairness, and explainable user interfaces. The safety culture within organizations comes from management strategies that include leadership commitment to safety, hiring and training oriented to safety, extensive reporting of failures and near misses, internal review boards for problems and future plans, and alignment with industry standard practices. The trustworthiness certification comes from industry-wide efforts that include government interventions and regulation, accounting firms conducting external audits, insurance companies compensating for failures, non-governmental and civil society organizations advancing design principles, and professional organizations and research institutes developing standards, policies, and novel ideas. The larger goal of effective governance is to limit the dangers and increase the benefits of HCAI to individuals, organizations, and society.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The concept of self-driving chemical laboratories builds on top of two technologies: robust artificial intelligence models that translate synthesis designs into executable instructions, potentially incorporating instrument feedback, and robotic workstations capable of executing those procedures seamlessly and without human intervention. Here we present RoboRXN, a cloud-native framework that unifies transformer-based retrosynthesis and chemical action extraction or prediction models with a commercially available synthesis robot and in-line high-resolution LC–MS. Across more than 3000 actions autonomously executed, we analyzed in details 33 reactions distributed among 10 single-step reactions and 9 multi-step campaigns. Eightythree percent of single-steps and all two-step routes succeeded without parameter adjustment; a branched four-step synthesis completed after one on-deck modification. Regardless of the overall success, we systematically encountered three recurring bottlenecks: hardware rigidity, execution-level data gaps, and slow physical feedback, which are seldom reported in the literature, despite being common to many commercial platform design. We delineate how each failure surfaced, quantify its impact on yield or throughput, and outline engineering and data-centric remedies. By publishing both the successes and the blind spots, we hope to redirect community effort from one-off demonstrations toward robust, transparent, and widely adoptable AI-driven laboratories.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Accurate and robust localization remains the fundamental bottleneck for truly autonomous robotic systems, despite decades of progress in probabilistic estimation and SLAM. This paper provides a critical and comprehensive review of mobile robot localization across sensing modalities, estimation paradigms, and deployment domains, covering ground, aerial, and underwater platforms. Beyond a descriptive survey, we explicitly analyze the limitations and trade-offs of existing approaches. We introduce an updated taxonomy that spans classical proprioceptive and exteroceptive sensors, emerging technologies such as 4D imaging radar and event cameras, and infrastructure-based positioning systems including GNSS and Ultra-Wideband. We revisit the evolution of localization algorithms, from Bayesian filtering techniques (EKF, UKF, and particle filters) to modern graph-based SLAM frameworks and tightly coupled multi-sensor fusion systems. Particular emphasis is placed on the recent paradigm shift toward learning-based and neural implicit approaches, including NeRF-SLAM and Gaussian Splatting, highlighting both their transformative potential and their current impracticality for real-time deployment. Unlike previous surveys, this work provides a unified cross-domain perspective while critically examining scalability, robustness, computational cost, and real-world deployability. We identify key unresolved challenges, including long-term consistency, operation in degraded environments, and the integration of semantic understanding into localization pipelines. Furthermore, we propose standardizing evaluation metrics with a formal Trajectory Completeness formulation to expose tracking brittleness. Finally, we outline future research directions toward resilient, certifiable, and truly autonomous localization systems, emphasizing the critical transition from passive estimation to Active SLAM in unstructured environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomous agents are transforming the discovery and optimization of solid electrolytes, a class of materials crucial to the safety and performance of next-generation batteries. This review summarizes recent progress in integrating machine learning, molecular dynamics, and density functional theory within closed-loop or semi-autonomous workflows that accelerate the evaluation of ionic conductivity, electrochemical and chemical stability, and processability. Data-driven frameworks now accelerate the screening of sulfides, oxides, and halides, while phase-field and multiscale models have provided mechanistic insight into dendrite formation, interfacial degradation, and chemo-mechanical coupling. Autonomous laboratories that combine robotic synthesis, in situ characterization, and Bayesian optimization further enable closed-loop experimental discovery. Despite this progress, challenges remain in data quality, model interpretability, and the limited autonomy of current systems. Future development will rely on five key directions: (1) constructing interoperable multiscale databases, (2) developing explainable and data-efficient algorithms, (3) tightly integrating computation with experiment, (4) exploring new solid-electrolyte chemistries via agent-driven optimization, and (5) fostering coordinated global collaboration among open AI agents. Together, these developments mark a transition from empirical discovery to an integrated, self-improving research paradigm, where AI evolves from a predictive assistant into an active collaborator that learns, reasons, and supports materials innovation alongside human researchers.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-throughput yeast engineering is being transformed by biofoundries that integrate automation, artificial intelligence (AI), and standardized workflows. This review examines how these facilities accelerate strain development through the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle, with advances in genome editing, phenotypic screening, and predictive modelling. It highlights Australia’s involvement through the Australian Genome Foundry, Idea-BIO, and the CSIRO Biofoundiry and explores global efforts to overcome reproducibility and standardization challenges. Despite progress, key barriers remain, including protocol variability and integration of AI tools. We also highlight the opportunity for a shift toward autonomous, self-optimizing ‘self-driving labs’ that transition from DBTL to Design-Build-Deploy cycles. The future of yeast engineering depends not only on technological innovation, but also on the harmonization of international standards, data governance, and ethical safeguards. If fully realized, the convergence of robotics, AI, and synthetic biology will redefine yeast engineering, leading to step changes in strain performance for a variety of important products, thus enabling economic and sustainable biomanufacturing at scale.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Over the last years collaborative robots have gained great success in manufacturing applications where human and robot work together in close proximity. However, current ISO/TS-15066-compliant implementations often limit the efficiency of collaborative tasks due to conservative speed restrictions. For this reason, this paper introduces a deep-learning-based human–robot–safety framework (HRSF) that aims at a dynamical adaptation of robot velocities depending on the separation distance between human and robot while respecting maximum biomechanical force and pressure limits. The applicability of the framework was investigated for four different deep learning approaches that can be used for human body extraction: human body recognition, human body segmentation, human pose estimation, and human body part segmentation. Unlike conventional industrial safety systems, the proposed HRSF differentiates individual human body parts from other objects, enabling optimized robot process execution. Experiments demonstrated a quantitative reduction in cycle time of up to 15% compared to conventional safety technology.</jats:p>

A crucial aspect of physical human–robot collaboration (HRC) is to maintain a safe common workspace for human operator. However, close proximity between human–robot and unpredictability of human behavior raises serious challenges in terms of safety. This article proposes a risk analysis methodology for collaborative robotic applications, which is compatible with well-known standards in the area and relies on formal verification techniques to automate the traditional risk analysis methods. Abstract:
Abstract The development of automated work machine systems towards autonomous operation is proceeding rapidly in different industrial sectors. The aim of the study was to explore the current situation and possible differences in standardization supporting the development in different industrial sectors. The existing ISO and IEC standards and work items related to autonomous machinery were reviewed as well as activities in international industry groups regarding automation and autonomy of machinery. In general, the current standards are made mostly for machine manufacturers, but the views or responsibilities at worksite level are not considered. Three different approaches for safety concepts for different operating conditions were identified. One of them relies on onboard safety systems including sensor and perception systems for indoor applications. One guides to separate and isolate the autonomously operating machinery and to use access control to the autonomous operating zone. The third one is relying mainly on the machine operator’s ability to understand the situation and to react correctly according to the available information. From technology point of view there seems to be a gap between the safety requirements set in standards and the state of the art in currently available technology.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Autonomous mobile robots, including humanoid robots, are entering industrial plants faster than the standards written for them. No published type C safety standard covers dynamically stable industrial mobile robots, while Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and Directive (EU) 2024/2853 attach a defined legal consequence to the absence of evidence about how a machine behaved. This document specifies the component that produces that evidence, the Independent Conformance Monitor: eleven requirements in normative form, each traced to a legal obligation or a physical constraint and each with a conformance procedure a third party can execute. 2. Power-loss gravity drop test (measure sag distance by pose and payload)
3. Controlled stop before de-energizing (command park pose then cut power)
4. Pi reboot recovery test (what happens during and after reboot)
5. Collision force measurement (at worst-case pose and speed)
6. Safety laser scanner / perimeter detection (if added)
7. SOP walkthrough and training verification

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Test ID | Test Name | Standard/Source | What to Measure | Instruments | Minimum Repetitions | Acceptance Criterion | Records to Keep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| V-01 | E-stop functional test—magnetic supply switch | IEC 60204-1 stop categories; ISO 13850 principles; ISO 13849-2 validation; ISO 10218 protective stops. Category 0 immediately removes actuator power, after which an unbraked arm may descend. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000027) | Time from actuation to supply loss; stopping time and distance; gravity-driven travel after power removal; hazardous motion; latch/reset and restart behavior; independence from Pi, CAN, network and IoT software. | Two-channel oscilloscope or logic analyzer monitoring switch and supply voltage; current probe; 60–240 fps calibrated video; ruler or laser distance meter. | At least **3 per condition**: empty and maximum intended payload, worst horizontal/downward poses, and maximum permitted speed; test each actuator and foreseeable fault separately. (pqac-00000002) | Every actuation removes power without software; hazardous commanded motion stops; reset alone cannot cause restart; the complete stopping-plus-drop envelope remains contained without impact, pinch, spill or payload release. Until passed, the switch must not be credited as an E-stop. | Protocol and date; wiring diagram; component IDs; raw traces and video; pose, speed, payload and tool; each result and maximum; anomalies, corrective actions and reviewer signatures. |
| V-02 | Power-loss gravity-drop characterization | ISO 12100 risk assessment and system-level validation under real-use conditions; back-drivable actuators can move under output loads after de-energization. No published PiPER-specific drop data were found. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029) | TCP and joint displacement from power loss to rest; peak downward speed; time to contact; final pose; payload retention; effects of pose, payload, mains loss, relay opening and CAN/controller failure. | High-frame-rate camera with calibrated scale; tracking software; optional joint/CAN logging and accelerometer; noninterfering catch sling, foam stop or support. | At least **3 per pose–payload condition**; use **5** where variation exceeds 10% or results approach a boundary. Test no load, typical load and maximum intended load in home, maximum-reach and task-critical poses. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) | No person can occupy the measured fall/sweep envelope; no contact with printers, cameras, containers or enclosure; no payload release. Operation near people requires a support, brake, counterbalance or exclusion enclosure containing the worst result plus uncertainty and margin. | Joint angles and pose images; payload mass and center of mass; synchronized video; calibration; displacement, peak speed and settling time for every trial; mean, range and maximum; updated hazard-zone drawing. |
| V-03 | Controlled stop and supported park before de-energizing | IEC 60204-1 category 1 concept: controlled deceleration followed by power removal; an unbraked arm still requires a supported or gravity-stable final state. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006) | Command-to-stop time and distance; arrival at supported park; independent park confirmation; residual motion after de-energization; parking timeout or failure response. | Controller/CAN logs; supply-voltage trace; calibrated video; independent park sensor if installed; mechanical cradle or support. | At least **3 per initial pose–payload–speed condition**, including maximum reach and payload; inject each foreseeable parking timeout/failure at least once. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027) | Routine shutdown reaches and confirms the supported park before power opens; subsequent sag creates no pinch, spill or collision; failure produces a latched fault and prevents restart. Emergency isolation must remain immediately available. | State diagram; timeout values; initial/final joints; command, standstill, confirmation and power-off timestamps; post-power displacement; fault-injection results; configuration and software hashes. |
| V-04 | Raspberry Pi reboot and recovery test | Complete-system behavior must be tested against predetermined criteria under real-use and foreseeable-fault conditions. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000031) | Arm and relay behavior during commanded reboot, watchdog reset, Pi power interruption, network loss and CAN loss; reboot duration; boot-time outputs; stale-command replay; reconnection and job-resume behavior. | Pi serial/system logs; CAN logger; supply/relay voltage trace; video; network capture; watchdog log. | At least **3 per failure mode**, both stationary and moving; repeat empty and at maximum intended payload in the worst gravity-loaded pose. | Reboot cannot unexpectedly remove support torque while unsupported, issue motion, replay commands or resume a job. Recovery requires deliberate local reset/start after communications, pose, payload, enclosure and safety status are verified. | Hardware/software versions; injected fault; synchronized logs and timestamps; relay/CAN states; trajectory and payload; restart steps; pass/fail and corrective action. |
| V-05 | Collision force and pressure characterization | ISO/TS 15066 body-region limits and PFL guidance; tests should reproduce risk-assessment contact scenarios using biofidelic instrumentation. Commercial devices have differed by about 5% on average and up to 10% under matched settings. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000043) | Peak transient force and force–time curve; quasi-static force for trapping scenarios; pressure/distribution; speed, pose and contact geometry at closest-to-base or otherwise highest-effective-mass configurations. | Preferred: calibrated ≥1 kHz load cell or force gauge behind a body-region-appropriate spring/damper pad; Fuji Prescale or calibrated pressure film. Validate low-cost sensors against known loads; inexpensive resistive sensors have lost linearity above 150 N. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000047) | **5 per contact condition** after setup qualification; use **30** for one representative condition when establishing repeatability. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) | Every individual result plus measurement uncertainty remains below the applicable force and pressure limits. Otherwise reduce speed, remove sharp geometry, add padding/guarding or exclude people. A bare hobby load cell is screening evidence, not formal ISO/TS 15066 conformity evidence. | Sensor model/serial and calibration; uncertainty; sampling/filter settings; pad stiffness/damping; body region; fixture and geometry; pose, speed and payload; raw curves and film scans; peaks, mean, SD and maximum. |
| V-06 | Safety scanner/perimeter protective-stop test, if added | ISO 10218-2 safeguarding; ISO 13855 separation distance; COVR protective-stop testing. Published SDL work validated scanner-triggered stops and checked safety-zone dimensions. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000039) | Detection and total response time; stopping time/distance; final clearance; field coverage and blind spots; warning/reduced-speed/stop sequence; clear-zone and restart interlocks. | Calibrated test piece; oscilloscope or logic analyzer; video; laser meter with stated error below 5% or motion-tracking system. (pqac-00000002) | At least **3 per approach direction, field, intrusion point, speed, pose and payload**, including boundaries, corners and foreseeable occlusions. | Worst final position plus uncertainty and margin remains within the protective separation distance; every intrusion produces the specified stop; no automatic restart; authorized restart only after the zone is clear. | Scanner configuration/checksum; field drawing; response/stopping data; final distances; test points and directions; raw traces/video; bypass and reset/restart results; approval. |
| V-07 | SOP walkthrough, training and emergency drill | Validation should cover intended use, system limits, users and training; training should include programming, troubleshooting and emergency response. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000038) | Ability to inspect, start and stop safely; actuate E-stop; respond to sag/drop; isolate energy; clear jams safely; handle spills or broken vials; identify signage and hazards; report incidents and near misses. | Approved SOP/checklist; written and skills assessment; scenario cards; training roster; observation form; isolation hardware. | One successful walkthrough and one observed emergency drill for **every authorized user**; repeat until all critical steps pass unprompted. | All safety-critical steps completed correctly; no interlock bypass; user understands that reset does not initiate restart; only trained, named personnel operate or recover the cell; SOP and hazard analysis approved before research use. | Controlled SOP revision; trainee/instructor and dates; competency results; drill observations; authorization level; refresher date; incidents, near misses and corrective actions. |
| V-08 | Periodic and change-triggered re-verification | Risk assessment and validation should be repeated after mitigation and when tasks, environment or operators change; ongoing monitoring should include close calls, incidents and feedback. No cited standard sets one universal interval. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032) | Continued E-stop, interlock, park, reboot and restart performance; drift in stopping/drop/collision results; wiring/configuration changes; damage or wear; sensor contamination; training currency and incident trends. | V-01–V-07 protocols and instruments; configuration/version comparison; maintenance, training and incident logs. | Functional E-stop and interlock check **before each operating session**; documented inspection **monthly**; repeat V-01–V-04 **at least annually** and after any relevant change, repair, crash, firmware/software update or incident; repeat V-05/V-06 after geometry, speed, payload, tooling or safeguarding changes. ### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Approach | Example Devices/Studies | Cost Range | Force Accuracy/Repeatability | Pressure Capability | Limitations | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Commercial biofidelic pressure-and-force measurement device (PFMD) | GTE Kolrobot 300N, GTE CBSF-75 Basic and CoboSafe; interchangeable springs and damping elements simulate body-region mechanics | Exact prices not reported; highest-cost option in this comparison | Three commercial devices differed by about 5% on average in a robot pre-study and by up to 10% under matched bench conditions. Five-trial average SD was 0.4–1.4%; one 30-trial condition had peak-force SD below 1%. | Yes, typically by separate pressure film or compatible pressure sensor; CoboSafe uses scanned and calibrated Fujifilm Prescale film | Results depend on spring rate, damping, moving mass, fixture stiffness, geometry, alignment and filtering; commercial-device agreement does not itself establish traceable accuracy | (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000047) |
| Low-cost load cell plus spring/damper pad | Calibrated load cell or force gauge mounted behind a body-region-specific elastomer and mechanical spring; research analogue of the mass–spring–damper PFMD | Exact prices not reported; potentially low to moderate, depending on load cell, amplifier and data acquisition | No general accuracy figure was published for a DIY assembly. Commercial comparisons show that even nominally similar compliant devices can differ by 5–10%, so calibration of the complete assembled system is necessary; sampling of at least 1 kHz and documented filtering are appropriate benchmarks | No intrinsic pressure measurement; add calibrated pressure film or a pressure array | A bare load cell is not biofidelic. Compliance, damping, moving mass, bandwidth, fixture rigidity and dynamic calibration must be characterized; suitable for screening unless validated against a reference PFMD | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000047) |
| Fuji Prescale pressure-sensitive film | Fujifilm Prescale/FUJI foil used with CBSF-75 or CoboSafe; coloration is scanned, calibrated and evaluated in software | Exact prices not reported; relatively inexpensive per test, but consumable and requires scanning/calibration | Does not measure force or the force–time curve. Quantitative pressure accuracy was not reported in the cited studies; interlaboratory work found pressure results sensitive to small alignment and edge-contact differences | Yes—time-integrated pressure distribution and estimated maximum/local pressure | Single-use; no transient waveform; limited pressure range, saturation risk, added contact stiffness and strong sensitivity to curvature, edges, placement, scanning and calibration | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) |
| Low-cost resistive force sensor | Inexpensive resistive sensors reviewed by Hartmann et al. | Exact prices not reported; lowest-cost sensor class considered | Reported to lose signal linearity completely above approximately 150 N, with correlation to a certified reference load cell collapsing under dynamic impact | Generally point or area-force sensing rather than validated pressure mapping | Unsuitable as sole evidence near common ISO/TS 15066 transient-force limits unless independently calibrated across the full dynamic range; affected by hysteresis, saturation and uncompensated dynamic effects | (pqac-00000008) |
| Pendulum test bench | Instrumented pendulum used by Zimmermann et al. and Samarathunga et al. to compare and characterize biofidelic sensors at nominal energies such as 0.5 and 1 J | Exact prices not reported; low to moderate if fabricated in-house, excluding the reference sensor | Repeatable excitation rather than a sensor itself. Zimmermann used five impacts per setting; actual energy differed from nominal by up to 5%, while device SD averaged 0.4–1.4% | Only when the impacted PFMD includes pressure film or a pressure sensor | Does not reproduce robot controller response, effective mass or full kinematics; pendulum mass, velocity, geometry, alignment and energy require calibration. Best for sensor comparison and dynamic characterization, not stand-alone cell conformity | (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) |

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions

        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:

    InterventionalAssignment:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->

List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->

target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run a small university cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, no joint brakes, no certified safety functions; it sags when power is removed), driven over CAN from a Raspberry Pi, with its supply switched by an IoT relay and a magnetic-switch E-stop on the supply. Our current state: the E-stop has never been tested; rebooting the controlling Pi cuts the arm's power mid-move and the arm drops; a hazard analysis and SOP are drafted but not reviewed; unattended runs are not allowed yet; the arm shares an enclosure with Raspberry Pi cameras and will tend consumer 3D printers and move vials, SEM stubs and sealed powder jars near people. An earlier literature answer already covered safety architecture (hardwired dual-channel E-stops that bypass software, safe states versus de-energizing, retry policies, no unattended combustible metal powder). We now need the verification side: how to test and document that what we built actually works, at university-lab cost.

Question.
(1) Test procedures and acceptance criteria for emergency-stop and protective-stop functions on small robot arms: what IEC 60204-1 (stop categories 0, 1, 2), ISO 13850, ISO 13849-2 (validation) and ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 require or recommend; how stopping time and stopping distance are measured (instruments, number of repetitions, worst-case pose and payload); and published examples of such tests on cobots or low-cost arms.
(2) Arms without brakes: published measurements or analyses of what happens on power loss (drop distance and speed under gravity, by pose and payload), and mitigations used on low-cost or hobby arms (mechanical brakes, back-drive resistance, controlled-stop before de-energizing, rest poses, UPS-backed controllers, supported park positions).
(3) Collision testing with inexpensive instruments: measuring transient and quasi-static contact force and pressure against ISO/TS 15066 body-region limits using force gauges, load cells, pressure-sensitive film or low-cost biofidelic pads, with reported accuracy versus commercial collision-measurement devices; and measured collision forces for low-cost arms (PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, myCobot, xArm Lite, UFactory or similar) if any exist.
(4) Risk assessment and documentation for robots in academic research labs: what university EHS programs (published policies, guidance documents or papers) require before a robot cell runs, including attended versus unattended operation, training, signage, interlocks, and periodic re-verification; and any incident reports involving low-cost or educational robot arms.
(5) A minimal, defensible verification plan for a cell like ours: which tests to run first, with how many repetitions, and what records to keep.

Prefer peer-reviewed sources and published standards or official guidance from 2010 to 2026; flag preprints, theses and vendor documents. For each claim give the DOI, standard clause or URL and quote the supporting sentence. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Since 2010, industry has been using a new type of robot capable of interacting with workers during production or simply sharing the same workspace with them. They are called collaborative robots, or cobots. Cobots differ from conventional robots with respect to machine-worker interaction; they accompany workers, assist them and help them perform tasks. However, this technological change also brings with it new risks, especially in production: collision risks (since humans can come into contact with cobots), risks of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) (even though a cobot may be designed to prevent such problems, operators must learn to handle it properly to limit or prevent them), psychological and social risks (human stress related to cobot movements and work pace), etc. An exploratory study was conducted to investigate these issues. The purpose of the study was, first, to make occupational safety recommendations regarding the implementation of robots in a collaborative setting and, second, to suggest ways to inform stakeholders about the issues involved in implementing cobot installations.

There were two parts to the study: a theoretical part focused on examining plans and a practical part focused on the actual situation in the field. The purpose of the first part was to assess how the robot’s safety functions, which are processed by safety-related electronic boards, ensure operator protection within the framework of the four modes of collaborative operation established by standard ISO 10218:2011: (1) safety-related monitored stop, (2) hand guiding, (3) speed and separation monitoring and (4) power and force limiting. According to standard ISO 13849-1:2015, a safety function of a machine is a function of the machine whose failure can result in an immediate increase in the risks to a person’s physical well-being. For example, the emergency stop on a machine is a safety function. The purpose of the second part of the study was to gather feedback on taking safety into account in collaborative robot integration projects in Quebec. Feedback was collected from three types of participants: collaborative robot users (employers), integrators and workers involved.

The theoretical part was conducted by analysing the technical reference material for three robots: one designed to be collaborative and two conventional robots converted into cobots. In addition, a brief case study illustrated the implementation of a cobot installation based on the analysis. The field part of the study was carried out by observing cobot installations in four companies and conducting semistructured interviews with the participants concerned.

The case study of the theoretical part showed that to make a mode of collaborative operation safe, a number of safety functions must be combined, depending on the robot. The theoretical part revealed, in particular, that the performance level set by the manufacturer for a safety-dedicated controller is not a guarantee of the overall performance level of the safety function processed by the controller. The controller’s electronic board only performs the “signal processing” part of the safety functions. An employer that procures a collaborative robot equipped with a controller that meets the performance level set in the standards should not assume that the cobot’s safety functions will necessarily meet the requirements of the standards. A robot’s safety functions often need to be supplemented by adding an input device, such as a presence-sensing device. In some cases, environmental constraints may be an overriding factor in the choice of a sensing device. Choosing the right device is crucial, because if its safety performances are below those of the processing part, the safety function will be less reliable. The requirements in the standards recommend so-called safety devices.

The field part of the study revealed that cobotics is in its infancy in Quebec. Only one of the four companies visited had a cobot installation that was up and running. The other three were in the process of cobot integration. Other companies contacted by the study team when recruiting participants for the visits were either planning to procure a collaborative robot or were still thinking about how to integrate it into their production process. The companies visited chose their cobots on the basis of (1) their low cost compared with that of a conventional robot, (2) quick return on investment, (3) being able to reassign workers to more rewarding tasks, (4) space constraints and (5) potential occupational health and safety (OHS) risk reduction. Thus, to judge from what we observed, companies are turning to cobots not necessarily to meet a need for human-machine interaction in production, but rather for financial, spatial and OHS reasons.

The integrators we met confirmed that designing a cobot installation is a complex task because the technology is very new and involves some very specific safety requirements. The most difficult step, they say, is the risk assessment. Often, it was limited to risk identification. But to know whether a robot can be used in a collaborative context, at the very least the risks of the future installation must be estimated in order to determine the minimum required performance level. The performance level of the safety functions must be equal or superior to this minimum and be consistent with the analysis of the risks associated with collaborative operation.

Last, for safety to be a decisive factor when determining needs and integration, it must be included in each planned functionality of the installation. This inclusion must be implemented through a close dialogue involving the employer, the integrator and workers. From what we observed, workers were not very involved in the process of determining needs and integration. Given this low degree of worker participation in risk assessment, which in itself is a complex step, we are now proposing to conduct research on the cobot-related risk assessment process, by incorporating analysis of worker activity. In addition, regarding risk reduction, some aspects are worth investigating further, particularly (1) presence sensing, in modes 1 and 3, with non-safety devices and (2) the applicability and acceptability of the force limit values given in technical specification ISO/TS 15066:2016. Worker proximity to the robot during production requires a risk evaluation focusing on possible contact. In sum, using collaborative robots does not systematically mean that protective measures are no longer necessary. Risk assessment is always needed at the integration stage, as manufacturers’ reference manuals and cobotics standards specify. Depending on the degree of acceptability of the risk in question, protective measures may well be required.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The safety of robotics and automation technologies is a significant concern for stakeholders in Industry 5.0. Ensuring cost-effectiveness and inherent safety requires applying the defense-in-depth principle. This paper introduces a novel risk-informed design framework for functional safety, integrating function-centered hazard identification and risk assessment via fault tree analysis (FTA). Demonstrated in the design of a semi-automated agricultural vehicle, the framework begins with a function-centered hazard identification approach (F-CHIA) based on ISO 12100. It examined design intents, identified hazard zones, and conducted task and function identification. Foreseeable functional hazardous situations are analyzed, leading to functional requirements and the identification of relevant directives, regulations, and standards. The F-CHIA outputs inform the functional safety analysis, assessing the required performance level and deriving specific requirements for software, hardware, and human operators using FTA. The functional requirements derived from F-CHIA are more systematic than traditional methods and serve as effective inputs for functional safety analysis in human–robot collaboration applications. The proposed framework enables design teams to focus on enhancing factors that improve functional safety performance levels, resulting in a more thorough and effective safety design process.

Abstract:
Arm support systems provide support throughout daily tasks, training or in an industrial environment. During the last decades a large diversity of actuated arm support systems have been developed. To analyze the actuation principles in these systems, an overview of actuated arm support systems is provided. This overview visualizes the current trends on research and development of these support systems and distinguishes three categories. Therefore, the actuated arm support systems are classified according to their user environment, namely: ambulatory, rehabilitation and industrial. Furthermore, three main actuation principles and three mechanical construction principles have been identified.

Abstract:
The agricultural sector is constantly evolving. The rise in the world’s population generates an increasingly growing demand for food, resulting in the need for the agroindustry to meet this demand. Tractors are the vehicles that have made a real difference in agriculture’s development throughout history, lowering costs in soil tillage and facilitating activities and operations for workers. This study aims to successfully design and build an autonomous, electric agricultural tractor that can autonomously perform recurring tasks in open-field and greenhouse applications. This project is fully part of the new industrial and agronomic revolution, known as Factory 4.0 and Agriculture 4.0. The predetermined functional requirements for the vehicle are its lightweight, accessible price, the easy availability of its spare parts, and its simple, ordinary maintenance. In this first study, the preliminary phases of sizing and conceptual design of the rover are reported before subsequently proceeding to the dynamical analysis. To optimize the design of the various versions of the automated vehicle, it is decided that a standard chassis would be built based on a robot operating inside a greenhouse on soft and flat terrains. The SimScape multi-body environment is used to model the kinematics of the non-back-drivable screw jack mechanism for the hitch-lifting arms. The control unit for the force exerted is designed and analyzed by means of an inverse dynamics simulation to evaluate the force and electric power consumed by the actuators. The results obtained from the analysis are essential for the final design of the autonomous electric tractor.

Abstract:
Safety is essential for robots in unknown environments, especially when there is physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). Control over energy, or passivity, is an effective safety mechanism. However, when the control algorithm is implemented in a discrete-time computer, computation and communication delays readily lead to loss of passivity and to instability. In this paper, a way to make the actuators aware of the energy that they inject into the system is presented. Passivity and stability are then always guaranteed, even in situations of total communication loss. These Embedded Energy-Aware Actuators are a model-free passivity and safety layer that make complex robotic systems dependable, well-behaved and safe. The proposed method is validated in simulation and experiments.

Abstract:
Enhancing the transparency of high-transmission-ratio linear actuators is crucial for improving the safety and capability of high-force robotic systems having physical contact with humans in unstructured environments. However, realizing such enhancement is challenging. A proposed solution for active body weight support systems involves employing a macro–mini linear actuator incorporating an electrorheological-fluid brake to connect a high-force unit with an agile, highly back-drivable unit. This paper introduces the use of an electromagnetic (EM) brake with reduced rotor inertia to address this challenge. The increased torque capacity of the EM brake enables integration with a low-gear-ratio linear transmission. The agile translation of the endpoint is propelled by a low-inertia motor (referred to as the “mini”) via a pulley-belt mechanism to achieve high transparency. The rotor of the EM brake is linked to the pulley. Damping modulation under high driving force is achieved through the adjustment of the brake torque relative to the rotational speed of the pulley. When the brake is engaged, it prevents any relative motion between the endpoint and the moving carrier. The endpoint is fully controlled by the ball screw of the high-force unit, referred to as the “macro”. A scaled prototype was constructed to experimentally characterize the damping force generated by the mini motor and the EM brake. The macro–mini linear actuator, equipped with an intrinsic failsafe feature, can be utilized for active body weight support systems that demand high antigravity force.

Abstract:
Improving the transparency of high-transmission-ratio linear actuators is essential for enhancing the safety and performance of high-force robotic systems that engage in physical contact with humans in unstructured environments. However, achieving this goal presents significant challenges. A proposed solution for active body weight support systems involves a linear actuator design, combining a high-force unit with an agile, highly back-drivable unit, using an electrorheological-fluid brake. This dissertation introduces an approach that utilizes an electromagnetic (EM) brake with a reduced rotor inertia to address these challenges. The EM brake's increased torque capacity allows for integration with a low-gear-ratio linear transmission. The mini motor, with low inertia, drives the agile movement of the endpoint through a pulley-belt mechanism, enabling high transparency. The rotor of the EM brake is connected to the pulley, and damping is modulated under high driving forces by adjusting the brake torque in relation to the rotational speed of the pulley. When the brake is engaged, it locks the motion between the endpoint and the moving carrier, ensuring that the endpoint is fully controlled by the high-force unit's ball screw, known as the "macro." A scaled prototype was developed to experimentally analyze the damping force generated by both the mini motor and the EM brake. This macro–mini linear actuator, which includes a built-in failsafe feature, can be applied in active body weight support systems that require significant antigravity forces.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents an integrated experimental and modeling framework to
investigate human–robot collision dynamics involving a collaborative manipulator (KUKA
LBR iiwa 14 R820). A dedicated impact test prototype was developed to reproduce con-
trolled contact scenarios between the robot and human body analogues under various
dynamic conditions. The experimental setup enables the acquisition of synchronized force,
velocities, and displacement signals during contact events. This data are used to calibrate
and validate a set of contact models, ranging from classical formulations such as Hertz
and Hunt–Crossley to more recent supervised machine learning models. The proposed
methodology allows a quantitative assessment of model accuracy and physical consistency 
in replicating real collision phenomena. Furthermore, the effective mass of the robot along 
its kinematic chain is estimated to compute impact energy and predict the interaction
severity according to ISO 10218-1/2:2025 safety limits. The results highlight the trade-off
between model complexity and predictive capability, offering alternative guidelines for
collision severity evaluation in collaborative robotics applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This article discusses creating a methodology for the asymmetric measuring of values and processes of collision forces and pressures of the collaborative robot dependent on time. Furthermore, it verifies the usefulness of this methodology in practice by successfully performing the experimental measurement and verifying the possibility of using these results by analysing and stating the collaboration level for a robot of the given type. According to the suggested methodology, the measurement results are a specific output based on real measured data, which can be easily rated and can quickly determine the collaborative level of any robot. Measurements were aimed at determining the values of pressure and force with which the robot acts at certain speeds related to distance from the base. Due to the controlled symmetrical impact of the robot on the measuring device, the transfer of energy from the robot to the human body was guaranteed. In theoretical terms, this article primarily provides the assembly of the theoretical foundation of the collaborative environment between humans and robots, and a comprehensive overview of the possibilities of using the technical specification ISO/TS 15066:2016 when deploying a robot in collaboration with humans in a collaborative environment. This new information is highly valuable for both manufacturers and users of collaborative robots. The presented article analyses the possibilities of measuring collaboration and safety elements in cooperation with a robot. The most significant practical benefit is the presentation of a methodology for measuring robot collaboration and verifying its functionality by conducting experimental measurements of robot collaboration according to this methodology. The measurement was performed on a robot made by Universal Robots, model UR10. The measurement coordinates were stationed in a way to create a spatial measurement model. Boundary coordinates of the spatial model were as follows: [450; 200], [450; 500], [850; 200], and [850; 500]. Collisions were measured at 8 different speeds for each coordinate (20 mms−1, 50 mms−1, 100 mms−1, 200 mms−1, 250 mms−1, 300 mms−1, 350 mms−1, and 400 mms−1) to enable the observation of changes in accordance with speed. The measured values indicate a significant fact: the closer the collision is to the robot’s base, the higher the collision forces. An important aspect is that the measured values were only for speeds up to 400 mms−1, which is a very low value for industrial use to meet the desired cycle time. It can be stated with absolute certainty that speed has the greatest impact on collision force values. The speed of the collaborative robot arm can therefore be considered a limiting factor for use in industrial applications with a requirement of a short cycle time. Focusing on the results of the measured values, it can be stated that a new finding is the correct design of robotic movements in relation to possible contact with humans is crucial. The result of the measurement according to the proposed methodology is a specific output of realistically measured data, which can be easily evaluated and the level of collaboration of any robot can be quickly determined. The measured data will also serve as a basis for further processing and preparation of new simulation software. It will be possible to use the intended software for detecting and predetermining the safe asymmetric movements of the collaborative robot already at the stage of production preparations, unlike the method of measuring force and pressure on robots which can be used until the time of implementation into production. In the future, this software may also allow users of collaborative robots to easily and quickly evaluate the robots specified.
